Canadians Lean European on New Cars, Many Warm Up to Electric Vehicles
13 photos
Photo: Renault
Commissioned by Clean Energy Canada, a new survey from Abacus Data suggests that 47 percent of Canadians prefer a Euro-leaning new car market, especially when it comes to electric vehicles and smaller footprints than what they're accustomed to from the United States of America.
Be that as it may, 21 percent would rather see more American influence on Canadian roads. The margin is better than two to one, and the people who commissioned the polling read it as demand the current shelf does not fill. Abacus Data surveyed 2,762 adults online between September 18 and September 23, weighted to match census data on relevant metrics, and made it work with a 1.86-point margin error.
Before picking a direction, respondents were asked by Abacus Data to think through what each one would mean for the brands, models, segments, and electric options actually available to them at the time of the survey. What the remaining share of the sample wanted goes unstated in the survey, leaving the status quo with whatever is left after the aforementioned 47 and 21 percent are counted.
The demand behind the preference is electric, and it appears to be growing. 48 percent of Canadians now say their next automobile is likely going to be fully electric, up three percentage points from the 45 measured in April 2026 and last year. Age bends the curve a lot, with youngsters aged 18 to 29 more inclined to go electric than 30 to 44-year-olds.
What holds many potential EV customers back is diversity. Among likely electric vehicle buyers, 42 percent would rather wait for more Chinese alternatives to reach Canadian dealers. 37 percent believe there are too few electric pickups on offer, and they're completely right on that one. However, the lack of demand for such vehicles is clearly visible in Q3 2026 releases from all manufacturers who offer electric trucks in Canada.
Photo: Renault The gap between what buyers know about the product and what the market sells also deserves some attention. Upfront price consistently ranks as the most prohibitive barrier to going electric, hence the pitiful demand for electric trucks. With a bit of luck, Ford's all-new Fathom will democratize the electric pickup for both the US market and Canada.
The survey also found that Canadians are poorly informed about how far prices have already come. 60 percent of potential buyers are at least somewhat aware that new EVs can be purchased in the $30,000 to $40,000 range, but only one in five is very aware of those options. Used electric vehicles fare much worse. Awareness of the $5,000 federal rebate on eligible new EVs stands at 62 percent.
69 percent, meanwhile, know that EVs are generally cheaper to own and drive. Said figures suggest that a good chunk of the affordability question is an information problem. All in all, 2027 will be a pivotal year for Canada's electric vehicle market due to the arrival of the Fathom and the introduction of additional Chinese models, including a rumored pair of models from Geely .
The Abacus Data survey, as presented by Clean Energy Canada, carried a small test of whether the Canadian appetite for European rules is actually real. Canadians were told that European law requires public chargers to accept credit/debit cards without an app, which is completely different from Canada's app-happy charging infrastructure. 69 percent of respondents agreed that Canadian chargers should be required to work the same way.
And finally, politics also point in the same direction. European Commission prez Ursula von der Leyen, who is particularly vilified across Europe if you are to believe the social media nonsense spewed by Russian bot farms, invited Canada in September 2026 to become the bloc's first associate member. The EU-Canada summit at the end of October 2026 could very well advance the relationship, bringing Canada closer to Europe's auto industry.

Roche has gained access to a genetic obesity approach from China’s Rona Therapeutics for up to $100 million in upfront and near-term payments.
Swiss pharma giant Roche has tapped China’s Rona Therapeutics for an RNAi-based activin receptor-like kinase 7 obesity drug candidate, securing another foothold in an already crowded obesity space.
The global licensing deal, announced Tuesday , includes up to $100 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments and as much as $1.06 billion in milestones down the road.
Roche has already been a member of the mainstream obesity peloton, licensing GLP-1, GIP and amylin candidates and pouring money into manufacturing capacity for injectables, all in the name of becoming a top three player in obesity. Now, with the addition of Rona’s platform approach, Roche joins a growing subset of companies looking for a genetic solution to obesity through inhibition of the activin receptor-like kinase 7 (ALK7) protein.
ALK7, which is coded by the ACVR1C gene, is found in adipose tissue and has been discovered as a target for obesity and other metabolic diseases. Quieting the protein could reduce fat deposits while preserving muscle. Muscle loss has been an ongoing side effect of many GLP-1 drugs, and leaders from both Roche and Rona underscoring the importance of optionality for the future of weight loss drugs.
Rona CEO Stella Shi touted the company’s extrahepatic delivery platform as a means for bringing an ALK7 drug candidate to the table. An extrahepatic delivery method allows for genetic agents like mRNA and siRNA that would normally accumulate in the liver to remain outside of the organ to drive a therapeutic effect.
Other drugmakers in the ALK7 race include Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals, which in January revealed interim results from a clinical trial of its drug candidate called ARO-ALK7, which demonstrated a 14.1% placebo-adjusted reduction in visceral fat. Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, an experienced siRNA drug developer, has also embarked on early clinical trials with its own ALK7 candidate, ALN2232.
Meanwhile, GSK, like Roche, has opted for a licensing approach, in May linking up with Chinese biotech SiranBio for $55 million upfront and up to $1 billion total. As part of the deal, GSK will gain access to SA030, SiranBio’s long-acting siRNA oligonucleotide that targets the ALK7 receptor.

Network Aviation Group has appointed Hendrik Falk as vice president of the Americas, ahead of Paul Umpleby’s retirement at the end of the year.

He previously served as Chapman Freeborn’s senior vice president of cargo for the Americas, overseeing its North American cargo division and expanding its regional sales presence.

A Bombardier Global 6500 aircraft. (Bombardier via US Army)
WASHINGTON — The US Army’s new spy plane program remains on track, but if lawmakers delay passing a 2027 budget, the service will not be able to move into production as planned, a senior defense official warned.
“We actually are still completely on cost with the program and completely on schedule, which is somewhat rare across the department,” Andrew Evans, the director for the Strategy & Transformation Office inside the Army’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence shop (G-2), told Breaking Defense.
“However, the CR [continuing resolution], which is out of our hands, does complicate that. So next year at this time, will I be able to say the same thing? I don’t know,” he added on the sidelines of the Annual Association of the US Army conference.
RELATED: Can’t start, won’t start: Over 150 new military programs face delay under CR
So far, the Army is moving out with development of three High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System (HADES) prototypes — Bombardier Global 6500 jets that Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) is outfitting with different tech packages. The first prototype, according to Evans, is slated to be delivered around the January 2027 timeframe and will be used in an operational demonstration to ensure that “everything from aperture to analytics is all connecting.” After that it will be made available to Pentagon leaders to decide how to use the collection asset.
“They will tell us what their priority is, and the asset will fly to that area and begin collection operations,” Evans said.
The second prototype should be delivered roughly six months later, and the third one, which is “significantly advanced from the first two,” is slated for delivery in 2028.
But after those three prototypes, the Army had been eyeing HADES production aircraft and planned to ink a deal with SNC around the start of 2027. However, lawmakers have not approved a fiscal 2027 defense spending bill and are funding the government on a continuing resolution through early December. A spending bill could take even longer given the upcoming midterm elections and Pentagon plans to work with lawmakers to reconfigure the spending request.
If those talks and budget slip further into 2027 or the defense leaders want to pull HADES funding for other priorities, then a production contract could be put on ice.
“We are ready to move in on the ‘27 [plan to] award a production contract for HADES; We cannot do that … until we clear a CR,” Evans said.

Redesigned 2027 Audi Q7 Scores 100 Percent for Essential Driving Controls in Euro NCAP Testing
7 photos
Photo: Euro NCAP
Redesigned on the Premium Platform Combustion, the new Q7 has left Euro NCAP's testing facilities with five coveted stars under its belt. One of its biggest wins comes down to physical controls, with the luxury-oriented sport utility vehicle scoring 100 percent for essential driving tasks and 80 percent for comfort/infotainment controls.
Euro NCAP says the controls in question are easy to see, nicely placed, and usable without inducing headaches. Shots fired at touchscreen menus, but hey, I like to hate touch-only essential controls as much as the next guy. Under the nonprofit organization's 2026 testing protocols, the 90 percent overall score for the Q7's use of buttons and switches matters a lot.
The tested controls are frequently used items, beginning with the indicators and the hazard light button. Others include the windshield wipers and washer system, the horn, and the eCall button. Euro NCAP claims these should be available through direct physical input instead of being integrated as digital controls in the central infotainment screen.
Although the 2026 testing protocols do not amount to a blanket rejection of touch controls, they do reward layouts that benefit ease of use and muscle memory. A buried digital menu requires the driver to take their eyes from the road for a valuable second or two, while an actual switch is extremely easy to recognize and get accustomed to.
Produced in Slovakia, the 2027 model year Audi Q7 was tested by Euro NCAP in left-hand-drive TDI 220 kW guise. A lesser diesel is available, with Audi listing 180 kilowatts on deck. Converted to imperial units, make that 295 and 241 mechanical horsepower.
Photo: Euro NCAP Euro NCAP obviously tested the Q7 for safe driving, crash avoidance, protection, and post-crash safety, with the large SUV scoring 72, 77, 88, and 100 in these categories. To earn five stars, a vehicle does not require full marks in all four categories. The 72 percent score for safe driving exposes a few gaps, of which the lack of child presence detection as standard stands out.
The Q7 does not recognize occupants sitting out of position either. A front passenger could put their feet on the dashboard, and a vehicle this smart does not alert them about the safety risks associated with this position in the event of airbag deployment. Speed assistance was a relative strength, with Euro NCAP driving the Q7 for about 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) to test the system.
Over this distance, the Audi identified posted speed limits correctly in 87 percent of cases. Euro NCAP further explains that the Q7 performed well in side pole and barrier impacts, with its center airbag protecting the front occupants from slamming their heads against each other. The German sport utility vehicle from Slovakia is also good in terms of dooring.
That is when someone opens the door without checking the mirrors, potentially injuring a cyclist approaching from behind. Low-speed collision performance scored 68 percent, with so-and-so results for pedestrian and cycling in crossing and maneuvering scenarios.
Post-crash safety is the Q7's strongest category in the eyes of the Euro NCAP, clocking 100 percent out of a maximum 100. The organization gave it such a high score for the provided rescue information, eCall functionality, and provisions to help emergency crews extract occupants quickly and safely in the event of a crash. In certain situations, eCall provides information about the occupants and the impact to help responders assess the situation before arriving on the scene.

By Charlotte Goldstone
13 October 2026
Freight forwarders should focus on using artificial intelligence to capture lost gross profit and deliver more tailored customer service, rather than treating the technology primarily as a productivity tool, according to Erik Muttersbach, founder of AI software company Zauber.
Speaking on The Loadstar Podcast , Mr Muttersbach said AI could transform freight forwarding into a higher-value, higher-margin business over the next three to five years, with a growing divide between companies that adopt the technology quickly and those that struggle to keep pace.
Mr Muttersbach said 2025 saw a wave of AI start-ups and funding announcements, while 2026 has been characterised by companies running pilots and proofs of concept, alongside industry leaders committing to larger-scale deployments.
He expects the first results of these implementations to become visible in financial reporting next year, particularly in earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT), shipment volumes and customer retention.
The challenge, he said, is not simply implementing software but transforming organisations. For this reason, he said that CEOs must articulate how AI will improve the business and address employees’ concerns about job security and changing business models.
He highlighted that rather than using AI to increase productivity, forwarders should instead target opportunities to improve profitability. These include charging for waiting time, managing demurrage and detention cases more effectively, and improving allocation management by using earlier visibility of inbound volumes to make better use of carrier contracts.
AI could also help forwarders deliver on complex customer-specific requirements that have traditionally been difficult to manage consistently across global operations. Mr Muttersbach explained AI systems could draw on customer standard operating procedures (SOPs), previous correspondence, transport management system (TMS) data and operational expertise to ensure shipments are handled according to individual customer needs.
Historically, these requirements have often created additional work without being properly priced into contracts, while inconsistent knowledge across branches can result in service failures.
“There’s an opportunity to do incredibly individual customer service every single time,” he stressed, and underscored that forwarders that continue offering only standardised services risk losing their competitive edge as customers increasingly expect individualised service to become the norm.
While AI will not eliminate the need for human relationships, Mr Muttersbach expects roles to change significantly, with people focusing more on complex problems, customer relationships and strategic supply chain support.
On whether to build or buy AI systems, Mr Muttersbach recommended developing in-house solutions where a forwarder has a genuine strategic advantage, such as distinctive approaches to customer order management or carrier allocation.
More standardised processes, meanwhile, may be better handled by specialist providers with the experience and data to deploy solutions quickly and cost-effectively.
He also stressed the importance of integration: AI must have access to the same operational actions as human employees through APIs or EDI connections if it is to automate meaningful work.

Geely concluded its press conference at the 2026 Paris Motor Show with a "one more thing" announcement: Project KO11. The vehicle is not new, being known as the Geely Cruiser 700 in China, but its name bears more significance than the car itself. If you wonder what KO means in Project KO11, it's exactly what Geely plans for rival off-road brands like Range Rover and Toyota.
Chinese carmakers took over this year's Paris Motor Show, with no less than 20 brands on display. Geely seized the opportunity to make its first group-level appearance at Paris Expo Porte de Versailles. The highlights were the Geely Monjaro EM-i, the Link & Co 07GT, and the Zeekr 9X. However, the most talked-about show car was the "Project KO11," introduced as a "One more thing" at the show.
For those familiar with the Chinese car market, the Project KO11 looks identical to the Geely Cruiser 700, also known as Battleship 700, depending on the translation. It's a proper off-roader designed to rival the Land Rover Defender. Scratch that, it's actually designed to destroy it, which explains the "KO" in the Project KO11's name.
The only reason why Geely hasn't introduced the KO11 as the Cruiser 700 is that it hasn't yet settled on a name for the EU-bound model. Cruiser 700 might get it into hot water with Toyota's legal department, while Battleship 700 is not a great name for Europe, no matter how you spin it. What's certain is that the name won't matter, because it would pose mortal danger to the Land Rover Defender regardless.
The Chinese name reveals that the Project KO11 is a 7-Series model, which means it sits just below the flagship models. This means it will provide all the creature comforts someone expects from a luxury 4x4 vehicle. The design is typical for a classic off-roader, with a boxy shape, high hood line, and a swing-out tailgate with a spare wheel mounted on it.
Photo: Geely The KO11 is underpinned by the Geely Terrain Architecture (GTA), which uses an integrated frame construction. This combines a unibody structure with a heavy-duty cage frame, saving space and weight while maintaining high torsional rigidity. The Geely Cruiser 700 / Project KO11 is the first model to use this architecture.
The Chinese model uses an EREV powertrain that combines a 2.0-liter gas engine with three electric motors for a total of 1,113 horsepower in its most potent configuration. The 70-kWh Golden Brick battery uses Geely's Short Blade cells and promises up to 217 miles (350 km) of pure electric range based on the CLTC cycle. Lesser configurations are also offered, including a smaller battery and a 1.5-liter engine.
These configurations will most certainly not make it into Europe, due to local emission regulations that basically exclude EREVs. This means that the Project KO11 will be converted into a PHEV off-roader, unless Geely decides to ditch the combustion engine altogether and launch it with a bigger battery as an all-electric off-roader. Not impossible, but it would certainly compromise on range, as the Jeep Recon EV showed us already.
The Chinese Geely Cruiser 700 is already on the market, with prices starting at 179,800 yuan ($26,800) for the base model. This is powered by a single electric motor and uses the 1.5-liter gas engine as a range extender. Australia will also get the EREV off-roader under the rather strange name of Battleship 700. Europeans, on the other hand, will have to wait another year before Project KO11 launches.

While BNT113 failed to improve progression-free survival in patients with a type of head and neck cancer during a Phase 3 trial, BioNTech is holding out hope for an overall survival win—but analysts say that outcome is now “less likely.”
BioNTech’s recent run of bad luck with its mRNA cancer immunotherapy pipeline continued Tuesday, as the company reported that one candidate, BNT113, failed to significantly improve progression-free survival in patients with a type of head and neck cancer in a closely watched Phase 3 trial.
“Results add to a growing list of recent mRNA cancer vaccine setbacks including two discontinuations for autogene cevumeran in bladder cancer and colorectal cancer,” BMO Capital Markets wrote in a note to investors Tuesday morning.
BioNTech halted a Phase 2 trial of autogene cevumeran in colorectal cancer in August due to futility following a recommendation by an independent data safety monitoring board. This followed the discontinuation earlier this year of a Phase 2 trial for the asset in bladder cancer “due to the rapidly emerging treatment landscape and shifting standard of care,” the company said.
The most recent miss, announced on Tuesday , comes from the Phase 2/3 AHEAD-MERIT trial , which is testing the mRNA immunotherapy in combination with Merck’s Keytruda vs. Keytruda alone for the first-line treatment of metastatic HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). The trial, which has enrolled 358 patients, has dual primary endpoints: progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).
BioNTech shares wobbled upon market open on Tuesday, falling 5% to $90.88.

Despite the PFS miss, the German biotech isn’t giving up hope on the trial just yet, suggesting that a positive readout on OS could still render the trial a success. The trial will therefore continue on to evaluate OS, “completing the assessment with the potential of this treatment approach to help patients live longer,” BioNTech said in its press release.
“Under the trial’s pre-specified statistical design, a statistically significant improvement in overall survival would establish a positive trial outcome, even if the progression-free survival dual primary endpoint was not met,” the company clarified in its announcement. This is in line with the recommendation of an independent data monitoring committee, BioNTech added.
BMO agreed that overall survival could still be achieved despite the PFS miss but said so with “significantly reduced confidence.” The firm noted, “While improvement in overall survival is still possible, we view such a scenario as less likely given today’s PFS miss.”
Around one-third of HNSCC cases are associated with HPV infection, with the majority linked to HPV16, BioNTech said in its release, adding that there are currently no HPV-targeted treatments approved. BioNTech is hoping to change that with BNT113, which encodes a fixed set of antigens to specifically target two HPV16-derived antigens that are frequently expressed on HPV16+ tumor cells.
BMO noted that as an mRNA vaccine, BNT113 is designed to induce an immune response against those target proteins. “This response may take longer to fully deepen, supporting the possibility that AHEAD-MERIT misses on PFS improvement, but an overall survival benefit can still materialize over time.”
BNT113 and autogene cevumeran are part of BioNTech’s personalized cancer immunotherapy pipeline that also includes BNT116, which is currently in Phase 2 development for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and Phase 1 for NSCLC.
Autogene cevumeran scored a win in a small Phase 1 trial in April. The study showed that nearly 90% of participants with pancreatic cancer whose immune systems responded to the immunotherapy plus Roche’s checkpoint inhibitor Tecentriq and chemotherapy were still alive up to six years after receiving the last treatment. The combo is currently in a Phase 2 study , which is expected to be complete in January 2031.

With the weekly average retail diesel benchmark release delayed a day due to the Columbus Day holiday Monday, that lagging indicator is likely to show another decline even as most of the industry discussion these days has been decidedly bullish.
Since the Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration price was most recently published October 8, the futures price of ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) has been moving in its usual crazy volatility, a feature of the current market since the U.S. and Israel commenced military action against Iran at the beginning of March.
But the overall futures market trend in the last week has been higher. ULSD settled October 6 at $4.5694/gallon. Within two days it was more than $4.88/g. It then sunk to a settlement Monday of $4.7232/g, but it wasn’t clear that the Trump diesel deal had any impact; for all of the boasting President Trump did about the transaction, it was only down 1.52 cts/g on the day. (Permitting red dye diesel to be used over the road also has hit a regulatory maze and is largely being dismissed as well).
On Tuesday at 10:45 a.m. EDT, ULSD was turning in another typical day of volatility. It was at $4.8185/g, up 9.53 cts/g, or 2.02%. But it had been as low as $4.6431/g on the day, for a low to high swing at that point of about 17 cts/g.
Will Russia deal bring relief?
The DOE/EIA price to be released Wednesday will be the first since the Trump administration announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel, a transaction that has largely been dismissed as irrelevant to supply/demand trends (and the Tuesday upward movement at publication time suggests the broader market was dismissing it as well). The deal with Russia also has been criticized by some members of Congress and others as illegal.
While the DOE/EIA number used as the basis for most fuel surcharges is only a weekly number, and can be delayed during a holiday week, there are other price indicators about what’s happening at the pump.
The AAA daily diesel price recently completed a 17-day run where the national average fell every day. At the start of that slide on September 22, the price was $6.5276/g. When it ended Friday, AAA said the average daily diesel price was $6.2785/g. It moved up and down slightly the next four days and Tuesday was largely unchanged from Friday.
The DTS .USA average retail diesel price in SONAR Tuesday was $6.32/g. The latest DOE/EIA diesel price was $6.199/g, effective October 5.
Part of the volatility in the market the past few weeks has been the swing in reports about how much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz. Without the one definitive number for the market to agree on, that sort of uncertainty will lead to volatility.
Shipments need help
But even if the number is high, as long-time analyst Paul Sankey told CNBC in an interview , what’s getting out is not transiting through the free flow of tankers that was the state of play before the war started.
“It’s supplied at enormous military cost,” Sankey said. “That’s how you’re getting the ships through, also with the shuttle tinkering. That’s another level of cost.”
He estimated those costs are probably worth about $35/b.
Under the terms of the diesel deal announced by President Trump, Russia is to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the world market. At a conversion rate of 7.45 barrels of oil per metric tonne, the formula used by S&P Global Energy in its calculations, that works out to 2.235 million barrels.
The rest of the deal would be another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes soon after. At the conversion rate of 7.45 barrels per metric ton, that is 3.725 million b/d for the November quantity and double that for the supply to come after that.
U.S. daily consumption of all non-jet fuel distillates, according to the most recent report from the EIA, is about 3.65 million b/d. For the members of the OECD, which consists of most Western economies, daily diesel consumption is estimated at about 13 million b/d.
A report from S&P Global Energy quoted Masha Kotkin, a fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, as saying “the amount of diesel Russia can provide would be a drop in the bucket compared to global demand. If you are asking about US diesel prices, I don’t think it’s going to make a difference. It is not very much in the scheme of things.”
It’s the products, not the crude
The move by the Trump administration to secure additional diesel supplies ultimately goes back to the reality that even if flows out of the Strait of Hormuz are increasing, irrespective of whether they only got there through U.S. military support, consumers buy refined products, not crude.
In a separate CNBC interview , Ellen Wald of Transversal Consulting said markets have been able to avoid even higher spikes in price through a wide variety of steps, including drawdowns from strategic stocks. But that has limits.
“We have seen some incredible resilience in the market,” Wald said. “We’ve seen an ability to work around and for the market to find workarounds. But at a certain point, things are going to start to give, and we’re seeing that as prices are creeping higher and higher. Any attempts to bring them down that aren’t actual new sources of supply don’t really last.”

Beyond the latest Russian diesel deal, and before that the agreement by G7 nations earlier this month to release additional strategic stocks, reportedly after a U.S. threat to implement a diesel export ban if they did not, there are the broader stock releases that were agreed upon by the members of the International Energy Agency in March.
IEA executive director Fatih Birol on Saturday tried to give a push to the ongoing releases and have them go faster.
“Members that have not yet fully delivered the volumes pledged under the March Collective Action look to see if they are able to accelerate the remaining releases to fulfil this prior commitment, prioritising diesel,” he said in his statement. He also noted that “some members have already released greater volumes than they initially pledged in March.”

In the Pacific, a single bolt can become a giant headache and the source of months of delay. The bolt that Col. Scott Carpenter held up Monday during the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting belonged to a Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station turret, and it is back-ordered until February 2027.
At U.S. Army Materiel Support Command — Korea, the unit Carpenter commands, soldiers built the bolt through the drill-out process of subtractive manufacturing for a cost of $1.27, avoiding months of delay and saving more than $300 in the process.
As the Eighth Army in Korea builds out its logistics capability, it’s investing in advanced manufacturing with an eye to supplying spares, not only to local Army forces, but also to troops across the Pacific region .
“I want to be the advanced manufacturing center for INDOPACOM,” Carpenter said at an engagement with reporters at the AUSA meeting. “That’s my goal.”
Eighth Army officials spoke earlier this year about how establishing a Korea-based regional sustainment hub, or center for logistics, maintenance and supply, could cut down the burden and cost of long-distance sustainment. At a roundtable event Monday, Eighth Army Commander Lt. Gen. Joseph Hilber indicated the force was moving out to build that sustainment hub.
“Now, rather than taking equipment that might need a major overhaul and send it back to the United States, we’re looking at ways that we can overhaul it there in Korea and keep it in the fight longer. Keep it west of the [International Dateline] longer,” Hilber said. “That’s going to involve everything from some added manufacturing capabilities to additional repair capabilities that we’ve got in there in terms of being able to fabricate parts, being able to fabricate materials, and then being able to return that equipment back into the fight.”
The Eighth Army has already resourced maintenance support teams that cross service and regional boundaries, departing the Korean Peninsula to support the III Marine Expeditionary Force in Okinawa, Japan, and to Hawaii to support Army rotational units, Carpenter said.
Through additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, and subtractive manufacturing, or cutting a part out of a solid block of metal, the Eighth Army is manufacturing an increasing number of critical parts, Carpenter said. The materiel support command recently acquired a metal 3D printer and is now building out infrastructure to house it.
“But we think come January, February, the metal 3D printer [will be] in, and my goal is … I would like to get to a point where I can 3D print the bolt,” Carpenter said.
U.S. Army officers tour a South Korean navy shipyard to examine 3D printers used for their equipment on March 25, 2026. (Spc. Keli Luangrath/U.S. Army)
By next summer, he said, the Eighth Army is set to receive $3 million worth of advanced manufacturing machines, with some $10 million worth of additional machinery set to be requested in the Army’s fiscal 2028 budget.
“I’ll be able to print bumpers; I’ll be able to print doors,” Carpenter said. “These are not just desktop printers.”
Recently, he said, a Guam-based military unit requested an assembly that would have cost $36,000. The Korea-based team built it through subtractive manufacturing for $82.
Through a request system, Carpenter said, any joint forces member can now request a part and get routed to the Army’s logistics hub in Daegu, South Korea.
“If you’re the Marines operating in Okinawa and you need this bolt … I get this bolt back over to the Marine at a fraction of the cost, and a lot quicker than if they were to order through the supply system,” he said. “So again, we’re maintaining combat power inside the First Island Chain.”
Hilbert said some hurdles remained for the Eighth Army, including intellectual property restrictions with manufacturers; data-sharing to ensure the advanced manufacturing processes deliver components that are up to spec; and seamless connection into existing Army logistics systems not designed for these new modes of parts production.
“We’re continuing to work through those pieces to enable us to fix faster,” Hilbert said.

Global ocean container schedule reliability fell for a fourth consecutive month in September, dropping 2 percentage points to 27% on-time, according to Xeneta’s September Schedule Reliability Scorecard.
Average vessel delay rose to 6 days across all arrivals, up 2.4 days since the start of the second quarter.
The analyst said the deterioration reflects the cumulative effects of powerful typhoons that struck Asia from July through early September, combined with bunker-cost pressure and strong peak-season demand. It does not expect a firm floor in October as Asian trade disruption continues.
Asia trades deteriorate
Asia-linked services recorded some of the worst performance, with the Far East-to-Europe trade collapsing to 4% on-time and an average delay of 9.9 days. That was the lane’s worst monthly result since September 2021, when on-time performance reached 3% during the Covid pandemic.
Asia-to-North America reliability was unchanged at a dismal 20%, but average delay increased 0.8 days month over month to 6.9 days. Xeneta said Chinese port congestion is increasingly translating into berth-arrival delays for shippers in Europe and North America.
The rate environment compounded the operational pressure. Xeneta’s spot-market average for China to the U.S. West Coast reached $7,717 per FEU in early October, more than four times the $1,778 recorded in September 2025 and 8% above the start of September 2026. Long-term rates rose 26% month over month to $3,649 per FEU on Oct. 1.
Carriers post delay highs
Every carrier tracked by Xeneta posted its highest average delay of the past 12 months in September. Four carriers also reached 12-month lows in on-time arrivals: CMA CGM at 30%, Cosco ( 1919.HK ) at 18%, Hapag-Lloyd at 45% and Yang Ming ( 2609.TW ) at 4%.
The performance spread between carriers narrowed to 43 percentage points, from 45 points in August. Maersk (OTC: AMKBY ), the month’s most reliable carrier, fell from 51% to 47%, while Yang Ming marked the low end at 4%.
Xeneta said the Gemini network of Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd — launched on a premise of on-time performance — declined more sharply than other alliances, falling from 70% on-time in June to 40% in September. Its weekly on-time rate dropped from 62% in the first week of August to 34% in the week ended Sept. 28, and partial data for the week of Oct. 5 showed 28%.
Singapore congestion doubles
Port congestion spread downstream from China into Southeast Asia. Singapore’s average daily vessel queue nearly doubled to 22 ships, while average wait time rose from 1.9 to 3.1 days, as the transshipment hub absorbed effects of congestion at Chinese gateways.
Southeast Asia recorded a 2.0-day average vessel wait, with 23% of vessels waiting. Africa remained the most congested region despite improvement, with a 2.5-day average wait and 32% of vessels waiting.
In Northeast Asia, 30% of vessels at port were waiting, and average wait rose 0.3 days to 1.6 days. Shanghai’s anchorage queue shortened from 101 to 86 vessels per day, although average wait lengthened from 1.9 to 2.7 days.
Capacity cuts may increase
Carriers blanked — cancelled or delayed — only 6% of planned capacity on Far East-to-Europe and 8% on Far East-to-North America in September, their third-lowest blanking levels in 21 months, as delays and pre-Golden Week demand absorbed available capacity.
However, announced blank sailings are set to rise in October to at least 17% of planned capacity on Far East-to-Europe and 13% on Far East-to-North America. Planned Far East-to-Europe capacity in October is the highest of any month in a 22-month window, leaving limited slack to offset delays through cancellations.
Xeneta advised shippers to allow more lead time for October bookings and to ask carriers which services will be protected from capacity cuts. It also warned that reliability, port rotations, unscheduled calls and capacity management should be central to carrier accountability discussions ahead of 2027 contract tenders.

source_document.body:
El Teniente’s Rajo Sur open pit sits near the top of the mountain surrounding the complex. ( Image courtesy of Codelco | Flickr. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 13, 2026
A snow avalanche that killed two subcontractor workers at Codelco’s El Teniente mine on Sunday has added to mounting supply concerns in Chile, as extreme weather, labour disputes and operational setbacks threaten output across the world’s largest copper producer.
The workers were inspecting the mine’s open-pit area, where operations had already stopped because of bad weather, the state-owned company said in a statement Sunday . Authorities are investigating the circumstances of the accident.
Located in the Andes Mountains about 75 km southeast of Santiago, El Teniente is the world’s largest underground copper mine.
The incident follows a series of disruptions across Chile. A recent study by GEM Mining Consulting estimated that an average 5.2% of annual production at the operations it assessed was exposed to operational risks.
Growing production risks
GEM’s risk study , dated September, assessed 14 major copper operations across eight categories, including labour disputes, weather, water availability, geological conditions and safety.
El Teniente ranked as the most exposed at 9%, followed by Los Pelambres at 8% and Escondida at 7.5%. Nine operations had at least one risk classified as high.
The 5.2% figure is a simple average of the operation-level scores, rather than a production-weighted estimate for Chile. The index assigns standard assumed losses to low, medium and high risk ratings based on public information from 2025 and 2026.
Severe storms have already disrupted Los Pelambres and Caserones , contributing to lower production forecasts.
Further weather risks loom. El Niño continues to strengthen, with a greater than 83% chance of strong to very strong conditions lasting through January to March 2027, the U.S. Climate Prediction Center said in its October outlook . The agency cautioned that associated weather effects aren’t guaranteed.
Operational pressures
El Teniente has also faced problems beneath the surface. Codelco suspended development of its Andes Norte section because of deep seismic risks, adding to production setbacks at the company.
Labour unrest is adding another layer of uncertainty. Antofagasta’s (LSE: ANTO) Centinela copper mine and two striking unions were scheduled to resume negotiations Tuesday under voluntary mediation.
The strike began Oct. 7 and involves 709 employees, or 22% of Centinela’s direct workforce. The mine produced 240,400 tonnes of copper last year.
Antofagasta said when the strike began that its projected production remained unchanged, despite operational disruptions.
Meanwhile, supervisors at BHP’s (ASX, LSE, NYSE: BHP) Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, have been in government-mediated negotiations aimed at averting a strike. A fatal accident temporarily halted operations in September.
Market expectations
Despite the growing list of disruptions, investment bank Panmure Liberum questioned how much of copper’s price strength can be explained by mine production losses.
Reported disruptions in 2025-26, including those at Indonesia’s Grasberg mine and Kamoa-Kakula in the Democratic Republic of Congo, amount to an estimated 350,000 to 400,000 tonnes of contained copper annually, according to the bank’s assessment cited by Reuters.
That represents 30% to 50% of published disruption allowances, the estimated losses analysts build into production forecasts to account for unplanned events.
Panmure Liberum consequently suggested that speculative and financial activity was probably the dominant driver of copper prices.
